claims.text: Ultrathin graphene interlayers act as barriers against dislocation creep in HEA multilayer coatings.
Graphene interlayers reduce time-dependent plastic deformation in HEA multilayer coatings.
Ultrathin graphene interlayers can be incorporated between HEA layers to form a nanolayered HEA/graphene material.
Elevated temperature and sustained loading create conditions in which creep is likely to occur.
Monolayer or ultrathin graphene forms an interface in a nanolayered CoCrFeNi/graphene composite.
A monolayer graphene interface can block crack propagation in a nanolayered CoCrFeNi/graphene composite.
Graphene interfaces stimulate or force dislocations to accommodate further deformation.
Dislocation accommodation at graphene interfaces retards creep deformation in the multilayer stack.
Graphene-interlayered HEA coatings will exhibit significantly lower creep strain than coatings without graphene.
Graphene-interlayered HEA coatings will exhibit a delayed onset of plastic deformation relative to coatings without graphene.
HEA multilayer coatings without graphene exhibit faster dislocation creep and greater time-dependent plastic deformation.
The proposed barrier effect requires graphene layers that are ultrathin, continuous, well-adhered, and compatible with the HEA matrix.
Excessive graphene thickness, discontinuity, or poor interfacial bonding reduces or eliminates the barrier effect.
The optimal graphene thickness, continuity, and interfacial adhesion for creep resistance are not yet specified.
A controlled comparison under identical elevated-temperature constant-load conditions can test graphene-containing coatings against graphene-free coatings.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in creep strain or delay in plastic deformation, or failure to observe dislocation blocking, would falsify the hypothesis.
